name: Angkor
info: Angkor, also called Yasodharapura, was the capital of the Khmer Empire in present-day Cambodia, founded under Yasovarman in 889 and the centre of a vast network of temples, reservoirs and canals until its sack by Ayutthaya around 1431.

facts.founded: The Angkorian period began around 800 CE with Jayavarman II; the city of Yasodharapura, centred on Phnom Bakheng, was built by Yasovarman, who ascended the throne in 889.
facts.where: Amid forests and farmland north of the Great Lake (Tonlé Sap) and south of the Kulen Hills, near the present city of Siem Reap in Siem Reap Province, Cambodia.
facts.known: The capital of the Khmer Empire; Angkor Wat, built between 1113 and 1150 by Suryavarman II; the walled city of Angkor Thom and the Bayon of Jayavarman VII; a system of roads, canals and reservoirs; the account of Zhou Daguan in 1296
facts.today: Angkor is a group of ruined temples and other monuments in Siem Reap Province, Cambodia, listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992 and administered as the Angkor Archaeological Park.

t: Jayavarman II began the Angkorian period around 800 CE, and Yasovarman built the city of Yasodharapura around the hill of Phnom Bakheng from 889.
Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1113 and 1150, and after the Cham sack of 1177 Jayavarman VII built the walled city of Angkor Thom and the Bayon over the ruins of the old capital.
Angkor was sacked by Ayutthaya around 1431 and nearly all of it was abandoned in the 15th century, though Angkor Wat remained a Buddhist shrine.
dyk: A study in 2007 using satellite photographs concluded that Angkor had been the largest pre-industrial city in the world by surface area, with an urban sprawl of at least 1,000 square kilometres.
ev: Jayavarman II declares himself universal monarch and god-king
Yasovarman ascends the throne and builds Yasodharapura around Phnom Bakheng
Suryavarman II begins Angkor Wat, which is built between 1113 and 1150
Cham forces sack the capital and kill the reigning king
Jayavarman VII takes the throne and builds Angkor Thom and the Bayon
The Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan arrives at Angkor
Ayutthaya sacks Angkor and its population moves south to Longvek
The École française d'Extrême-Orient begins the restoration of the site

sections.origins:
The ruins of Angkor stand amid forests and farmland north of the Great Lake (Tonlé Sap) and south of the Kulen Hills, near the present city of Siem Reap. Archaeologists dated the shift at Angkor from the Late Bronze Age to the Early Iron Age to 420 BCE, using radiocarbon dating of bivalve shells found in graves. The earliest Iron Age finds were iron and bronze spearheads, tool kits with iron-bladed knives, hoes for tilling land and bangles. Before the Angkorian period Cambodia consisted of a number of politically independent principalities, known to the Chinese as Funan and Chenla.

The Angkorian period began shortly after 800 CE, when the Khmer king Jayavarman II announced the independence of Kambujadesa (Cambodia) from Java. According to the Sdok Kok Thom inscription, his first capital, around 781, was Indrapura, near today's Kompong Cham. He became king of Kambuja in 790, moved to Mahendraparvata in the Kulen mountains and founded Hariharalaya, now known as Roluos. In 802 he declared himself a universal monarch (chakravartin) and a god-king (devaraja). Yasovarman ascended in 889 and built a new city, Yasodharapura, near Hariharalaya. It was centred on the hill and temple of Phnom Bakheng, and he also built a large reservoir called a baray. The name Angkor derives from the Khmer nokor, "kingdom", which comes from the Sanskrit nagara, "city".
sections.growth:
Between 900 and 1200 the Khmer Empire produced the architectural works known as Angkor. Most stand within an area about 24 km from east to west and 8 km from north to south, and around 72 major temples or other buildings lie there, with the remains of several hundred minor temple sites scattered beyond. Because medieval Khmer settlement was low in density and dispersed, Angkor had no formal boundary, but roads and canals defined an area of at least 1,000 square kilometres around the major temples, and in spatial extent, though not in population, it was the largest urban agglomeration in recorded history before the Industrial Revolution.

Angkor has been called a "hydraulic city", because a water management network stabilised, stored and dispersed water across the area. This network is believed to have been used for irrigation, to offset the unpredictable monsoon and to support the growing population. Scholars have debated whether the barays served to irrigate rice fields or were symbols of the oceans around Mount Meru. The size of the population remains a subject of research and debate; newly identified agricultural systems may have supported between 750,000 and 1,000,000 people. Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1113 and 1150, and Jayavarman VII, called the greatest of the Angkorian kings, oversaw the most prolific period of construction, including Angkor Thom, the Bayon, Ta Prohm and Preah Khan.
sections.rulers:
Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire, and its kings followed Jayavarman II in claiming the status of a god-king. An inscription dated 881 records that Indravarman I erected a lingam named Indresvara. Yasovarman ascended in 889 and built Yasodharapura, and Rajendravarman, whose reign began in 944, built Pre Rup. Suryavarman II came to the throne after defeating a rival prince in battle; an inscription says that he leapt onto his rival's war elephant and killed him. He built Angkor Wat as his personal temple mausoleum, and after his death around 1150 the kingdom fell into internal strife.

In 1177 the Cham, the neighbours of the Khmer to the east, invaded by water, sacked Yasodharapura and killed the reigning king. A Khmer prince rallied his people and defeated the Cham, and in 1181 he took the throne as Jayavarman VII. He adopted Mahayana Buddhism as his personal faith and made it the state religion. A Hindu restoration followed, beginning around 1243 with the death of his successor Indravarman II. In 1296 Zhou Daguan arrived at Angkor during the reign of Indravarman III. The Angkorian period lasted until the late 14th century, and Angkor first fell under Ayutthayan suzerainty in 1351. After the sack of 1431 the official capital later moved to Oudong in 1618 and to the present site of Phnom Penh in 1865.
sections.life:
Angkor was a religious centre and also a city that served all the needs of the Khmer people. All the remaining monuments except a few old bridges are religious buildings, because in Angkorian times all other buildings, including the king's residence, were built of perishable materials such as wood, "because only the gods had a right to residences made of stone". Most surviving inscriptions concern religious foundations, so the history of the state religion is easier to write than that of other parts of society. Roads and canals intertwined through the city in a grid-like pattern around the buildings, and the canals supported irrigation. At Ta Prohm a stone carving states that 12,640 people serviced that one temple complex, and about 300,000 agricultural workers have been estimated as necessary to feed the workers of the temples.

The Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan stayed at Angkor for a year from 1296 and wrote The Customs of Cambodia, about forty pages on religion, justice, kingship, agriculture, slavery, clothing, tools and commerce. He described a royal procession of soldiers, servant women and concubines, ministers and princes, and finally the sovereign, "standing on an elephant, holding his sacred sword in his hand". He found three religious groups: Theravada Buddhist monks with shaven heads and yellow robes, Brahmans, who were often high officials, and Shaivites, whom he called "Taoists". The bas-reliefs of the Bayon and Angkor Wat show the king's court, battles with the Cham and village life.
sections.crises:
The Cham invasion of 1177 sacked Yasodharapura and killed the king. Religious change brought its own damage. Under Jayavarman VII Hindu temples were altered to display images of the Buddha, and after his death the revival of Hinduism included a large-scale campaign of desecrating Buddhist images. Under Jayavarman VIII, a Shaivite iconoclast, the Bayon was made a temple to Shiva, and its central Buddha statue, 3.6 metres tall, was cast to the bottom of a nearby well.

The city had already been in decline in the 13th and 14th centuries. Ongoing civil wars with the Lavo-Khmer and the Suphannaphum-Mon dynasty of Ayutthaya were sapping Angkor's strength by the time of Zhou Daguan, who reported that the country had been completely devastated by such a war. After the Ayutthayan sack of around 1431 many statues were taken to Ayutthaya, and others went to the new centre of Khmer society at Longvek. Paleobotanical and stratigraphic evidence shows that the moat of Angkor Thom was no longer in use around that time. The main cause of the decline is unknown, and scholars have suggested the Ayutthaya invasions, the erosion of the royal cult under Theravada Buddhism, neglect of the waterways, disease, earthquakes, floods, and drought in the early 15th century, as tree-ring records show. During the 15th century nearly all of Angkor was abandoned, except Angkor Wat, which remained a Buddhist shrine.
sections.legacy:
Angkor never ceased to be known to the Khmer. Practice of Theravada Buddhism at Angkor continues to this day, and Angkor Wat was not completely abandoned in the 17th century: fourteen inscriptions of that century record Japanese settlements beside those of the remaining Khmer, and the best known tells of Ukondafu Kazufusa, who celebrated the Khmer New Year there in 1632. The Portuguese friar António da Madalena was the first recorded European visitor to Angkor Wat, in 1586. Henri Mouhot visited in 1860 and Anna Leonowens in 1865, and the archaeologist Louis Delaporte and the ethnologist Adolf Bastian then visited and made the site known in Europe.

From 1907 to 1970 the École française d'Extrême-Orient directed work at the site, clearing the forest, repairing foundations and installing drains. Scholars of the school, among them George Coedès, Maurice Glaize, Paul Mus and Philippe Stern, began the historical scholarship on which the present understanding of Angkor rests. Work resumed after the Cambodian Civil War, and since 1993 it has been co-ordinated by an international committee, while the Cambodian agency APSARA, created in 1995, carries out the Cambodian work. Some temples have been taken apart stone by stone and reassembled on concrete foundations. UNESCO declared Angkor a World Heritage Site in 1992. In 2007 a team using satellite photographs and other techniques mapped the extent of its water network. Angkor survives as ruins in Siem Reap Province.

summary: Angkor was the capital of the Khmer Empire in Cambodia, begun as Yasodharapura under Yasovarman in 889 and spread over at least 1,000 square kilometres with temples, reservoirs and canals. Angkor Wat and the Bayon were built there, and Ayutthaya sacked the city around 1431.

notes: SOURCES: only the city's own article exists (no history article). It is badly garbled in places (the Bronze Age paragraph, 'Angkor underwent many empire leaders', the 'Neglect' and 'Sustainable tourism' parts); I used only clear statements.

START: the article gives both 802 CE (Jayavarman II as universal monarch; the Angkorian period 'began in AD 802' in the lead, 'shortly after 800' in the history) and 889 (Yasovarman builds Yasodharapura, the city of Angkor proper). I used 889 for the city; circa false. The lead also says the name Yasodharapura derived from Krishna's foster mother and 'this temple was completed around 921': garbled, left out.

JAYAVARMAN II: the article gives 781 (Indrapura), 790 (king of Kambuja) and 802; his dates are as the article gives them, not reconciled. Mahendraparvata and Hariharalaya are named only as he moved/founded them.

END: 'generally set as around 1431' (sack by Ayutthaya); endCirca true. The lead also says Ayutthayan suzerainty began in 1351; the article does not say how the 1351 and 1431 events relate, and the lead's 'late 14th century' end of the period differs from 1431. The article says 'Suphannaphum-Mon dynasty of Ayutthaya' as the sackers; the lead says only 'Ayutthaya'.

Jayavarman VII's reign: 1181 accession; 'following his death' no date given. The Hindu restoration 'around 1243 with the death of Jayavarman VII's successor, Indravarman II'; the next king Jayavarman VIII. I did not give death dates for Jayavarman VII or Suryavarman II except 'around 1150' for the latter.

'Greatest of the Angkorian kings' is the article's judgement; I attributed it as 'called'. Calling Angkor 'the largest urban agglomeration ... prior to the Industrial Revolution' is the article's claim in spatial extent only; kept with that hedge. Left out: the claims about Paris and Egyptian structures, the 1,000,000-visitor figures, tourism, water-table, looting, and the 2013 Mahendraparvata find.

Population: only the 750,000-1,000,000 figure the article hedges ('may have supported'). The 12,640 at Ta Prohm and 300,000 agricultural workers are the article's, the latter from the passage on Coedès's religious argument; I wrote 'have been estimated as necessary', as the article does.
The article says Theravada was dominant at Angkor by 1296 (Zhou) and also that Theravada became dominant from the 14th century and made its appearance in the 13th; I did not state one date.

Angkor Wat: the article says it briefly became a Buddhist shrine under Jayavarman VII and remained a Buddhist shrine after the 15th century; its Vishnu image and Suryavarman's mausoleum are left out of the sections for space. The 'Hindu cosmology' of its walls is not described.

'Never ceased to be known to the Khmer': the article says Angkor 'was known to the local Khmer'. The user's rule about 'discovered' is respected; the article's wording that Europeans 'popularized' the site is used as 'made the site known in Europe'.
Present-day: the visitor figures are left out; the 'Angkor Archaeological Park' administration is from the article's historical overview.
